projectDesc.p: Encoded for the Experiencing War web site for the Veterans History Project.

samplingDecl.p: The recording of the interview with William Liddy was digitized.

editorialDecl.p: This transcription was encoded with minimal changes to the original text in an effort to preserve original content and idiosyncrasies of the person interviewed. Period language and terminology are also retained. Encoding is literal with regard to the transcriptionist's capitalization, punctuation, and spelling. Spelling errors are indicated with [sic]; however, recurring errors in spelling within a single document have been marked the first time and not subsequently.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Oral history of World War II veteran William E. Liddy. Mr. Liddy served in the U.S. Navy SeaBees with the 75th Battalion 36th Regiment. He served in the Pacific Theater yet his highest rank was Water Tender Third Class. I'm Tom Swope and this interview was recorded at Mr. Liddy's home in Kirkland, Ohio on March 9th 2005. Bill was 82 at the time of this recording.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Where were you living in 1941?

sp.speaker: William Liddy
sp.p: I was living in Euclid, on 196th Street, off Euclid Avenue.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: How old were you in '41?

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: 20? So were you out of school at that point?

sp.speaker: William Liddy
sp.p: Yes. I had been out of school. I'd been working as a draftsman for Parker Appliance for a while and then I went into the machine shop for the Ajax Manufacturing Company in Euclid on the apprentice program.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Do you have specific memories of December 7th, 1941?

sp.speaker: William Liddy
sp.p: Yes. The news came on the radio. It was a Sunday afternoon and my Dad said, "Would you listen to that?" He said, "I just knew it. I just knew it. We were gonna get involved." And they had it broadcast on the radio. We listened to it and we had also heard Jimmy Fiddler's broadcast on Friday evening prior to that when he said, "Why is it that nobody is investigating a fleet of ships?" It went past California going south, nobody knows who they are, where they're going or where they came from." That was a fleet that was going to Hawaii.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Really?

sp.speaker: William Liddy
sp.p: 'Cause they were following the Japanese currents which is a big arc from Japan, goes up past the islands almost to Alaska, then down our west coast and it takes them right in. They follow that current, it takes them right to Hawaii.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So, apparently somebody had spotted this fleet?

sp.speaker: William Liddy
sp.p: Jimmy had gotten the news flash that there was a fleet of ships that went by but he couldn't get any official reason or description of who they were.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Really?

sp.speaker: William Liddy
sp.p: But he just posed that question on the radio Friday night, and I heard that broadcast, and then Sunday we knew what the fleet was.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So you thought immediately of what he had said when you heard of the attack?

sp.speaker: William Liddy
sp.p: Yeah, his question that finite came back it night right way.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Oh boy?

sp.speaker: William Liddy
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So what was your personal reaction when you heard the news that we had been attacked?

sp.speaker: William Liddy
sp.p: Well we were just sitting around the house being lazy for Sunday, you know.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Uh huh.

sp.speaker: William Liddy
sp.p: Because back then Sunday was a day off and it was a day of rest, and you didn't do anything. You know, not like today, Sunday's just another day any more, but back then you be observed Sunday.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Was there any temptation on your part to run out and sign up the next day?

sp.speaker: William Liddy
sp.p: No, no, not really, I wanted to more or less feel my way around as to what branch of service I wanted to go in. I had my mind made up I was going into the service but shortly after that an article came out in the newspaper describing this SeaBee outfit. In the meantime I had gotten married and my father-in-law went with this civilian group that was going to Hawaii to rebuild pearl Harbor and that was original SeaBees but they didn't call them that then. It was just a civilian group going down there. The thing, trouble with that was being civilians they couldn't tell them they had to stay once they took them down there and so a lot of the guys just went down for the trip to Hawaii, and turn around and came back, my father-in-law was one of them, and then in order to keep a work group there they commissioned them under the Navy, as the Navy engineers. That way they could make them stay, and they knew they could get the work done then, and what they were out for was experienced people, tradesmen of all kinds, and that's what they were recruiting first and later on they were recruiting anybody to fill the compliments of the battalions. A battalion was about 1,200 men, officers, chiefs, enlisted men, but for the most part they were after tradesmen, so, because they needed them to just walk in and take over. They didn't want to have to train them. After a while they did train us in battle procedures, Navy, of course, trained us in marching, small arms, and so on, more or less to get us to respond to a command without thinking, which is what the military is all about. And that was called basic training, which took about six weeks.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So when did you go into the SeaBees?

sp.speaker: William Liddy
sp.p: When did I go in? I enlisted in October the 10th, 1942, and they didn't call me until December the 18th, and I was to report on the 22nd for transport to base camp and I got into Davis, Rhode Island which was the original base camp of the SeaBees, Christmas morning about two o'clock in the morning, so that was my indoctrination into the military. And they took us down and got us a mattress, mattress cover, a pillow and a blanket and then marched us up to our barracks through all the mud and water and so on, because they were still building the camp. And we got into bed at about three o'clock in the morning at the earliest, at five o'clock they turned on the lights and woke us up. So we had about two hours' sleep that night. And then from there on in it was, they didn't even have uniforms for us, we were wearing 3-C uniforms, remember the Civilian Conservation Corps? Okay, they outfitted us with those pants, shirt, jacket. But they did have the Navy cap and the Navy gloves and they did have shoes, but as far as the Navy uniform, we didn't even have the fatigues like I'm wearing now, because we were so new. And we took our basic training, there was a few days there where temperatures in Rhode Island were about 32 degrees below zero. Mighty cold to try and go outside and march in that stuff, and we eventually left there on Saint Patrick's Day and we were supposed to go to Chicago Pier, leave our gear there and go on leave, our basic training leave which was about ten days. And instead of going to Chicago Pier, we woke up one morning and we were in Indianapolis, and we were on dilapidated old antique passenger cars. The seats were straw. They had a coal stove in the back and kerosene lamps. And the inside and the outside were pure plank Philadelphia fencing, so you know how old those cars were. When we went in and walked that there was a half inch of black coal dust on the floor. You could see your foot prints in it. So we got in, we were supposed to be wearing our undress blues, soon as we got in there every one of us opened our sea bags and got out our fatigue clothes, and then we tore up the seats to make sleepers out of them because they were only coaches. When we finally got to Kansas City, the Army came aboard the train and condemned it, sent us over across the river to Kansas City, Missouri, or Kansas City, Kansas to the USO Center. We all took a shower, changed clothes, they gave us breakfast. When we came back there was all Pullman cars and that's the way we rode the rest of the way to Camp Park, California, and Camp Park is where you got in there at noon, no seven o'clock in the morning, at noon they let us out to go on leave. And of course I live in Ohio, we were in California, we had a ten-day leave and they give us three days' travel time. Well, it took three days to come home, so you used three days of your ten days going back (laughs). No fun. And when we got back there we were there about a month, I think, and then they transferred us down to Portland Amy, California which was our jump off spot to the South Pacific. We left on June the 9th, 1943 for the South Pacific. We had an escort out to the three- mile limit. And then that destroyer turned around and went back and every one of us, our hearts sunk down in our shoe tops because we're now alone and we were on a banana boat. It's called a Dell Brazil, but it was a fast boat. And on the 13th night out, this was a 16-day journey, and on the 13th day out, a Japanese submarine picked us up and as luck would have it, the man on duty spotted it, notified the British and we were doing a zigzag pattern, and he just flat out opened that ship up and went on a straight line, because he knew the sub couldn't catch him, especially submerged, because he had a six knot submerged, about nine knot surface speed and this ship was capable of doing 32 knots. So he knew he could outrun them. But in the process he burned up the bearings on one shaft because it was a twin screw ship so we were dragging a dead screw for the next three days until we got into New Caledonia, New Man, New Caledonia, where we got off the ship for the first time overseas and, of course, that ship had to go into repairs and get the bearings redone on that before they could go back to the States. And after that we spent about two months on New Caledonia. They packed us all up again, sent us up to Guadalcanal, we were on Guadalcanal for a short time. The first day there, we got in about noon. The water was as flat, as rippleless as could be. One of the sailors going by, I said to him, "How come the water is so calm?" He says, "There's a typhoon coming and we're right in the path." He wasn't kidding. By 2:30 that afternoon, it was just tearing everything up. The winds were straight across 125 miles an hour. There was no standing up in that. You crawled along wherever you were going. We had been unloading and one of the pontoon barges had a Marion shovel on one corner, a D-6 Cat on the other corner, and in between they had the boom for the Marion shovel. Well, the water got so rough that the barge came up out of the water, nose first, dumped the Marion shovel off the back end, went back down because the dozer was hitting. Out heavy dumped the dozer off (coughs). Excuse me. And then all the boom for the Marion shovel went off into 240 feet of water. Needless to say it stayed there, we never went after it (laughs). But that was terrific. There was a PBY base at Guadalcanal and they figured the water a little bit too rough for those PBY's and they will probably sink because most of the pontoon part of the ship was under water anyway. So they turned them around and tried to beach them. And we sent a couple dozers down there, put a line out to them and dragged nine of them back in on to the beach where we thought they would be safe. Well, seven of those nine were ruined just totally ruined and all they could was take them apart, send them back to a rear area for spare parts, they could never fly them again, so that's what a typhoon can do for you.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: How long did that last?

sp.speaker: William Liddy
sp.p: That lasted about two hours. Oh, and that time what devastation! The tops were broken right off palm trees. All that was left was the trunk because the palm fronds were always up at the very top anyway, the fruit and everything is up there. And it just took those tops right off and you could see those coconut trees bending almost 45 degrees one way and back and forth and that process the tops snapped off and was carried away. The natives went around the rest of the, after the storm was over, and gathered up those palm fronds 'cause that's what they used for their hut, their homes. They laid shingles out of them for the sides and the roof. They just laid flat and just overlapped them like we do with our shingles. Then we were on Guadalcanal for, oh, 'couple of months.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Well, working or training, or what were you doing at Guadalcanal?

sp.speaker: William Liddy
sp.p: We were more or less getting acclimated to the tropics, was what they were doing to us is and while we were on the Canal they had a couple of air raids but they were inconsequential because if you'll recall, Major Bong was in charge of a flight of P-38's and whenever there was an air raid his group took off from Henderson Field and they gonna make short work of them. There's no problem there. The P-38's could outmaneuver them. The Japanese weren't very adept at flying their own planes, I'll tell you that. They weren't adept at fighting a war either except maybe in China where they have the people outnumbered and outsmarted. Chinamen weren't fighters anyway. So-

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: What was your job with the outfit?

sp.speaker: William Liddy
sp.p: Well I had several jobs. I started out, I was fire department and then I went into water purification, and that's where I got my rating, Water Tender Third Class. But water purification was my mainstay after that, and when we weren't working on the stills because we used the stills over there and there wasn't this much underground water, so we used ocean water and purified it. Well evaporated it first, then purified it and then every once in a while we ran into a well. They always tried for underground water but it usually petered out before very long, maybe a month and that was if you used that up and the underground stream was gone. Unless maybe that was because more people tapped into it, but in between times I drove the truck with three of those trailer, tank trailers it's carried about 360 gallons. We took them off their axles and put them on the eight by eights along the bed of a deuce and a half GMC and hooked them all together with like a manifold water pipe and that gave us about a little over a thousand gallons of water and we'd go out and fill the lister bags for their work details, keep their water fresh for them because it didn't take long in the tropics. If you didn't have it chlorinated, for that water to start smelling even after purification, it would take on the germs out of the air and it will start to smell. And it wasn't good for them, so we'd empty the lister bag and put fresh water and clean it out, put fresh water. I made the rounds during the day like that. On Guadalcanal is where we had our first problem with dysentery and it happened because somebody had seen a cow and they shot it and brought it in, had our battalion doctor inspect it, look it over, and he said, "Sure, it's all right. Go ahead." So they skinned it, butchered it, and they had it for the evening meal that night. But that particular day was so hot that my friend and I that were on the water truck, were suffering from heat exhaustion, which gives you an upset stomach, dizziness, light headed. When it come chow time I said to him, "You going over to chow?" He said, "Nah, I don't feel like eating anything." I says, "Well I'm going over to see what they got for dessert anyway and something to drink." So they had tea, supposedly iced tea, and they had chocolate cake. So that's what I ate. About nine o'clock that night the dysentery took over and by the next morning my friend and I were the only two walking around. All the rest of them were either in the head or in bed moaning and groaning, and what they did for them was, they gave them a shot of morphine to stop it, and that morphine came in the form of a little tube with a needle right on the end of it. It was disposable, one shot. And a friend of mine from here in Cleveland, worked for Shaker Heights Hardware before he come into the service. He'd gone into the head and he was in there from well that night, three days later they hauled him out. He had weighed about 120 pounds, when they hauled him out he weighed 80 pounds and they took him to what was called a mobile hospital Mob 8. That's the last we had heard of him. We don't know what happened to him, lost track of him. Then from there, Guadalcanal, we went up to New Guinea. New Guinea had just been taken back and we went to a place called Noni Bay, which was a staging area where they brought in all kinds of troops, put them in barracks, waited for whatever outfit needed replacements came and got them there. So we were there for two or three weeks and we got the word that we were going to Australia on leave, but we has been in combat, but while we were in combat zone in Guadalcanal, there was sporadic firing there, battles, but nothing to write home about.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Were there still Japanese on Guadalcanal? Were there still Japanese on Guadalcanal?

sp.speaker: William Liddy
sp.p: Oh yeah, yeah, there's still Japanese but they were up so far that we didn't pay attention to them. But they would come down every once in a hill, cause a problem, whatever it was, in their line of fire, whether it will be the Marines or the Army, that was it. Took care of it, you heard about it the next day. So then while in New Guinea we were told we were going to Australia. We were running around getting uniforms from these guys that just came in. We'd all sent our stuff home, we didn't need it, and now we needed uniforms and we were going around, running around buying uniforms, taking them to the tailor and having the zipper put in the side under the arm, cut off at the two buttons and about 12 hours before we were supposed to muster for going to Australia, they changed the orders and we were all loaded aboard LST's the next day and headed for where we did not know. Island "X" again. And on the way up there our ship, the LST, started to break apart, crack down the sides on both sides right where the tank deck meets the super structure, so they had to pull in, delay us long enough for us to pull into Hollandia, unload from our LST onto another one and we did that from one afternoon to the next morning. We worked all night long and we were ready to go the next morning. Well when we were still in convoy, not knowing where we were going, we got word on the radio that the East Ohio Gas Company here in Cleveland, their storage facility had blown up and even the sewer systems were on fire because of the gas in the sewer system, and then the next morning we found out where we were, we were going into the Philippines, Leyte Harbor, which was kind of a unique sort of entrance. Only one ship could get through between where the two mountains came together in the water into this very big harbor, the capitol of Leyte, Tacloban. So the next morning we went in under smoke screen, and most of the day we were under smoke screen. We were under attack by the Japanese planes all day long. Finally, about five o'clock in the afternoon we had beached, ready to unload and everybody was still on alert, as far as the ship's crews was concerned they were all at their guns, and right over the mountain in front of our ship, a Japanese plane showed up and was headed for the docks that were off to our right, which held about three victory ships, or liberty ships and the gunner right next to where I was standing, 50 caliber, he worked the galley part of the ship's crew. He spotted that plane just as it broke over there and he opened up on it. We could see his bullets hitting that plane, and that plane drifted very slowly over the other side of the mountain and the next thing we saw is a big plume of fire where he had crashed so he got the credit for the kill, and then we unloaded and that night we didn't have time to dig fox holes or anything, there was an air raid by the Japanese, on that wharf area, pier, there were three ships there unloading and they had doused the lights and I just run for the closest ditch and laid down in that until the air raid was over and the lights came back on and we went back to work again (laughs). That's the way it went. You just waited them out and it was the same thing when we were at Bougainville. We'd be working day and night, my particular outfit, the 76th SeaBees, we built the fighter strip at what was called Torokina Point on Empress Augusta Bay, and the 77th Seabees, that guy from, Denny Franco, served, he was in the 77th. Here we are, he lived in Willoughby Hills and I live in Kirkland. We didn't know one another then. We were on the same island and probably about a mile and a half apart and that outfit, the 77th, built a bomber strip, so we had our share of problems there. The Japanese, they hauled a naval 68-inch gun, we watched them from on top of a tank we were building, a 10,000 barrel fuel tank for airplane fuel. We were up on top of that watching them carry that gun over the mountain and they were just body to body carrying that barrel and we didn't think anything of it until that first shell came in (laughs), then we knew what that gun was. Our intelligence wasn't all that great then, we were busy on the front line. So they were a group that lived on dope. They carried their dope right with them in little wicker baskets and that was also their food rations, rice.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: What kind of dope were they using, do you know?

sp.speaker: William Liddy
sp.p: They were using morphine and to the point where the 37th division had command of a top ridge of one of the mountains there and it was almost straight up and down on the one side facing the front line and these Japanese came across where there was crocodiles in this swamp. They waded through there, some of them were caught by crocodiles, lost limbs, died in the process. The rest had came through, they were screaming "bonsai." At the bottom of this hill there was a fence, barb wire fence, three wire, barb wire fence and it was only about well it was about like that, maybe 20 degrees. So the first Japanese that crawled over that fence started up the hill, got shot and rolled back down until the area was filled up to where the fence and hill side. They were rolling right all over the other bodies and they kept coming. One guy told me he was from down here in Cincinnati. He said he had a BAR and he was in a revetment dug into the hill sides covered over with sand bags, just room enough for the gun to peek out and he says, "I cut that man in half," he says, "his intestines fell out, and he kept on coming," he said, "That is scary, "he said, "What did you do? You killed a man and he's still running," so he says, "That's how desperate they were." So to show the Japanese that we could take them any time we wanted to we had PG soldiers that accompanied us. Us, I'm talking about the Americans, not my particular outfit, and they were spit and polish the creases on their shirts were so sharp you'd cut your finger on them. And they marched, it was like one person, you could only hear two steps when they marched until they got up to the front line, they stripped down to a loin cloth, a bow knife and a piano wire with handles on then, then they went over to want Japanese. They brought back three of their guns and we took pictures of them, sent them over to the Japanese and said, "This is what we can do any time we want to." But didn't convince them. We had loud speakers up on the front line, search lights up on the front line trying to convince them they were fighting a losing battle. So then they started bringing in reinforcements on the other sides of the islands. By that time we had the air field built and the planes were taking off, and going over and bombing, trying to get that 68-inch-gun in the hill sides. It was dug into a cave and double thickness coconut log door on it. They had it on railroad tracks and when they brought the gun out it was all done by manpower. They brought the gun out, fired it and the recoil rolled the gun back into the cave and closed the door. They only shot one shell every ten, fifteen minutes because it took that long to reload, get the gun back out there. But in the meantime when they were bringing in reinforcements they brought them in by barge because the water was shallow around there. We couldn't bring a ship in. We'd go over and bomb them, they never made it to shore and we even skip bombed that 68-inch-gun in the hillsides, still couldn't get it. So eventually we, you know, as I said before, we were trained military, and we had to take over the second line of defense because the right flank of our front line was starting to weaken, so we were put on second line of defense in case the first line came back, we were there but this happened why with the bombing and scraping on the right flank of the Japanese. The line held and we didn't have to do any fighting we were fortunate there, but that's how close we came to being in combat. Now the Japanese shelled our air strips, tried to anyway. They weren't very accurate. Well, one day they were shelling during the day and one shell landed on the revetment, or the median between the runway and taxiway. Didn't hurt the air strip but it did hit a 155 long Tom gun. All it did do actually was set the tires on fire because it was a two axles, dual wheels underneath it, and I was on the fire department at that time, and we were told to go down and put the fire out so we went down, set up our pump, got it run laid down on the bank of dirt around the gun and was pouring water on it when one of the Marines that were manning the guns come over and said, "Hey, you guys know you're laying on ammunition, don't ya?" What they did was they'd put their ammunition all around the gun and covered it with sand. We didn't know that we were laying on top of the ammunition. He said, "If a shell comes in, goodbye, boys," he says, "They hit us once, they're liable to hit us again." So here we are pouring water on this gun, trying to put the fire out laying on the ammunition. But we lucked out, they didn't fire any more this day, but we got it every night. They sent shells over to keep us awake. The idea was that if we worked all day and couldn't sleep at night, they can wear us down. It didn't work. And then they went what they called Washer Machine Charlie came over and he would fly right at the end of the search lights and beyond the anti-aircraft fire, just back and forth, back and forth. The reason they call him Washer Machine Charlie is the Japanese engine sounds like a washer machine (makes a grinding sound). Never did find out why. But then all of a sudden he would disappear. The guys on the search light would put their search light down, turn it off, turn it down, run for cover, because they knew he was coming in for a bomb run. He carries eight bombs, not very big bombs and most of the time they had what they called the grass cutters, which had about a six- to eight-inch projectile on the front of the bomb so that when that touched down it went off about sixteen- to eighteen inches off the top of the ground, cut you on the knees and they wanted to cripple you. They were called personnel bombs. Then he'd leave, but they'd do that every night starting about, oh, around eleven o'clock, twelve o'clock to about two in the morning, head make his bomb run and leave. but we'd put up this that several nights until we got the air base that they were come and we finally got that level by bombing. And now, you know, air fields were named ahead of time. Whether they were built by whoever and usually it was named after an army person. Well, tradition was that whoever landed on the air field first was the one that it was named after, so as soon as our planes that were passing over us going up for the bomb runs ahead of us spotted that field was in working order it radioed in and wanted to know if it was capable of landing a plane. Sure. Invariably, it will be a Navy pilot that had engine trouble and he'd come in and land. Well, the field was named after him, and when they got on the ground they found out he didn't have engine trouble after all (laughs). So one day we were, one of those guys came in on a Courseair and while he was on the ground for about, oh forty-five minutes there came a message that a Liberator was all shot up and was coming in for a crash landing, he only had one wheel and one engine, three of them has been shot out. Most of the rudder on the left side was gone and most of the crew has been killed, so we look up, and sure enough there was a Liberator up there we were looking at that one and so was be everybody else even in the tower. And the next thing you know, here it came in over the trees behind us and that Courseair was taking off because they figured they had enough time to get him off look out and see that plane up there and he was starting down the runway when the Liberator came and he was headed for the runway and by some miraculous maneuvering he hit the Courseair with the one wheel that was down, broke that off, now he has no landing gear and he slipped it over into the median and crash landed it there. Well, the guy that did the flying was the crew chief. He wasn't even a pilot, but he was taking his orders from that plane above on how to fly it and that co-pilot was still alive until he hit the ground and that finished the co-pilot but he walked out of it the only man alive is. That was some of the crazy things that happened.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So only one guy survived that on that plane? Only one guy came off that plane?

sp.speaker: William Liddy
sp.p: Only one guy came off it even the crew chief. That was the crew chief, yeah, all the rest of them had been kill by anti-aircraft fire and fighter plane fire gunners were all shot; pilot was shot, co-pilot was shot but still living and the crew chief was the only one alive so they hustled him right off before he could talk to anybody. That was on Bougainville.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: When were you on Bougainville? About when was that?

sp.speaker: William Liddy
sp.p: Um...

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: November 1st, 1943?

sp.speaker: William Liddy
sp.p: Yeah that's Bougainville, isn't it.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Yeah, Bougainville, November, okay?

sp.speaker: William Liddy
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: November '43 and Leyte was before that? Leyte was before that? Leyte was in...

sp.speaker: William Liddy
sp.p: Leyte was in '44.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: '44 that was after, okay?

sp.speaker: William Liddy
sp.p: Yeah yeah, we went in October. It was October the 23rd. We went in Leyte. Is it back on?

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: William Liddy
sp.p: And we went, we were on Leyte for, hmmm, maybe a month and moved across the strait to San Pedro straight to Samar. We set up a permanent camp like the one on Leyte was a temporary camp which means we just put up the tents, and that was it. Over on Samar we put up decks and put our tents 16 by 16, pyramidal tents, five men to a tent, and we were there for a couple of months. We were doing work all around the place, making roads building camps, all that sort of thing, they finally gave us our final assignment, moved us to a third called Kelly Cohen about two miles wide, about nine miles long and what we were supposed to do there was to build a 4,000-foot wharf for a naval supply depot and...

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Wow, a marginal wharf?

sp.speaker: William Liddy
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Uh huh.

sp.speaker: William Liddy
sp.p: It was 1,000 feet long, 60 feet wide, causeways out to it were 356 feet of fill, landfill, 40 feet of piling and decking, 40 feet wide. There were supposed to be nine of those jetties. We only had to build two of them to unload all the ships that were coming in there we could put in four or five ships at a time, and that was supposed to be the jump off spot and the supply depot for the invasion of Japan.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Um hum.

sp.speaker: William Liddy
sp.p: Okinawa kind of settled that and we didn't have to go into Japan, Okinawa, Iwojima, and we got the word August the 1st that the Japanese had finally surrendered and by September 9th I was coming home on rotation for a leave and I was supposed to go back and report back while aboard ship coming home which was a 21-day trip. The Navy point system came out and I qualified. There was 45 points in order to get discharged, I had 45 and a quarter points. So when I got off the ship I was headed for discharge and they took us in at Treasure Island which was the man-made island in San Francisco, man-made island in San Francisco harbor for the world exposition at one time, now a naval base. And from there they shipped us over, the SeaBees anyway, they shipped us over to Yerba Buena, it was called Goat Island, beautiful place, and being SeaBees, we had no duties. Regular Navy had to have, had to stand guard doing all that sort of things work details of all kinds. But the SeaBees were allowed out of camp by nine in the morning all you said to do was come back in by seven in the morning, find out what your assignment was, if there was going to be one or wait for your train, and I had to wait 13 days for the train home but luckily I had a aunt that had moved to San Francisco for the war because they got work in a war plant out there. Not only that their son was in the regular Navy but he was in a medical air base which was just across the harbor from San Francisco so I got out at nine in the morning and I'd taken a fatigue uniform into my aunt's place go into her place had a key to get in and it was on California Street which was almost straight up. The only thing that could travel on it was cable cars and underneath her apartment was the fire department and a pool table down there and we used to go down and shoot pool and some of the firemen were former service men that had been brought back already, and we swapped stories there, and they told us how San Francisco was laid out after the 1906 fire, earthquake and fire. Forty-nine square miles to San Francisco and there's one fire department for each square mile, yeah, there's 49 fire houses. END OF DISC ONE ---- BEGINNING OF DISC TWO And the water lines are metal up to intersections of streets, especially cross streets and there they had put in a tank right in the center of the two streets, a 1,000 barrel tank buried under the street and the lines into it were flex lines so that in the earthquake, the lines would still be connected, but the fire department had access to them. They would go over to this four foot cover, take it off, and had access there to the flex line to that 1,000 barrel tank under the intersections and that's the way San Francisco is laid out. So, all cross streets have got a tank buried in the intersection and there's access on all four sides for the fire department. So that was kind of interesting learning that. So after waiting ten days, about thirteen days, because I got into San Francisco on September the 30th, so it was about eleven days we got a train, finally, got a train home, got home to Toledo, is where they sent us in and we were to get discharged from there and they had so many people coming in at one time. They said, "Go home and come back tomorrow." So I hitchhiked with another guy and I, he was from Fairview Park. We hitchhiked to downtown Cleveland and he got a streetcar to his area and I got a streetcar to mine, and we bought a ticket coming back, we bought a round trip ticket. So we went to Toledo, got discharged on the 13th and then used the other half of our ticket to come back home. So I was back home again on the 13th, so I was in for three years, three days and I spent 28 months overseas.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: What was your reunion with your family like when you finally did get-- your reunion with your family -- what was that like when you finally got back?

sp.speaker: William Liddy
sp.p: Oh boy, that was something else, um, my wife was pregnant by the time I left for service. My son was born while I was on Guadalcanal, October of '43 and when I got home he was two years old. So he walked right up to me and says, "Hi, Daddy" (laughs). That was a shocker for you.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Um hum.

sp.speaker: William Liddy
sp.p: And the local butcher, whom I used to deliver papers to, he told my wife, he says, "When your husband comes home," he says, "You let me know." And so she went down and told him that I was gonna be home by the 13th. So he says, "Okay, you stop in. I got a package for you." So we went down and, of course, we exchanged pleasantries, shook hands. He congratulated me getting back and he handed me this package, and he says, "Have a good time." And we got home with all steaks, 3/4-inch thick steaks. So we went over to my folks' house and we had steak dinner, and everything that went with it, on him. That just about winds up.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Did you get -- how about mail call -- did you get a lot of mail from your family when you were overseas?

sp.speaker: William Liddy
sp.p: I got mail, and mail was rather sporadic. You got it once in a while and when you went in on an invasion any place it was a long time coming, and we knew we were getting mail whether they sent in the first DC-3 to pick up the wounded, badly wounded, to be taken back to rear areas. They always brought in the mail and we saw that DC-3 coming in. Hot dog! We got mail coming (laughs). And sometimes there would be a truck load for our, they had is and it was loaded.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Uh huh.

sp.speaker: William Liddy
sp.p: Right up to the top. Well, I told you about that cartoonist. There's a letter he sent me last year.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: He illustrated the envelope? That's great.

sp.speaker: William Liddy
sp.p: While I was over there, I worked in the, in my off hours, I worked in the publication of the daily news highlights and that cartoonist that I just mentioned there, this is all his cartoons for Easter, Christmas.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Oh, wow.

sp.speaker: William Liddy
sp.p: All that sort of thing.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Picture here of Miss Bougainville?

sp.speaker: William Liddy
sp.p: Yeah, that's something to write home about isn't it?

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Ha, ha. Did you have much contact with the natives on Bougainville, or the...

sp.speaker: William Liddy
sp.p: On Bougainville, we didn't because an awful lot of them were suffering from what they called Moomoo.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Um hum.

sp.speaker: William Liddy
sp.p: Elephantitis.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Um hum.

sp.speaker: William Liddy
sp.p: And we didn't want to get any of that so we stayed away from them.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Yeah?

sp.speaker: William Liddy
sp.p: We didn't even hire them like we did in the Philippines. We hired those people.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Um hum.

sp.speaker: William Liddy
sp.p: And they worked for a peso a day which was, in our money, was about 50 cents.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Um hum.

sp.speaker: William Liddy
sp.p: And for them that was, that was big money.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Yeah?

sp.speaker: William Liddy
sp.p: And they did just about anything we wanted for that 50 cents a day.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Were the Philippinos pretty nice to the Americans?

sp.speaker: William Liddy
sp.p: Oh, yeah, very nice, and of course it was nice to the people that you could understand.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Um hum.

sp.speaker: William Liddy
sp.p: Because they're Polynesian and the other islands were Malaysian and, of course, they all had their own language, whereas the Philippinos were was Spanish and a lot of our guys understood Spanish. We had some Mexicans in our outfit and we had some Indians, Native Indians. One in particular was a Paiute Indian from California. I worked with him quite a bit. Real nice fellow. But you run across every walk of life when you're in service and, of course, we had our share of the mountain boys that already brought their guitars and banjoes and harmonicas. We had song fests at night, poker parties. We even had our own gambling hall set up. They used the hospital tents, 40 by 100 and they set up a pool table, crap table, poker tables. Keep the guys home, because too often you get crap, floating crap games and it would just lead to trouble because somebody invariably introduced loaded dice. And the guy that slept right next to me on Bougainville there, he was over in the anti-aircraft battery which was right next to us, and when he got the dice and rolled them with his hand, he knew loaded dice when he saw them, and he fired those things off and he says, "We're taking our money and we're leaving." And there was enough of our guys that their guys are outnumbered and we walked away with the money. But up until then we'd been losing.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Did you have any particularly close buddies in the outfit?

sp.speaker: William Liddy
sp.p: Oh, yeah, one of them is now, he still lives up here in Albany, New York. He was a replacement, came in and he was kind of a lost soul, so I more or less took him under my wing and we've been fast buddies ever since. And I had one that lived down here in Streetsboro, and in fact, he started an allotment down here. The drive into it is named after him Wiencek Drive, off the 303 and I guess they built about 20 homes in there, he and his brothers. Their father had died right after, well let's see, his second younger brother was born, his father died, so what the boys did was built the house; not full-time, they did this in their spare time. They had regular jobs. When they sold the house they took a certain percentage of the profit among the boys and the rest of it went to support their mother. And this is the way they kept her going until she passed away and he just passed away about three or four years ago. But he was the guy I worked with on the fire department and water department and he and I, he was the other guy on Guadalcanal. He and I were the only two that were walking around camp. Boy, that's something else, a camp with 1,200 some people and it was quiet, you could hear a pin drop. Just the two of us, and we could holler back and forth from one tent to the other without any problem, you know.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Yeah?

sp.speaker: William Liddy
sp.p: That's awful.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: You mentioned some of the entertainment. Did you get any shows, any USO shows or anything?

sp.speaker: William Liddy
sp.p: Oh, yeah, we had Oklahoma.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Uh huh.

sp.speaker: William Liddy
sp.p: Showed up there and we had USO shows come in and we put on our own shows.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Oh yeah?

sp.speaker: William Liddy
sp.p: Yeah. We put on a show when we were here in the States, Rhode Island called "Pie In the Sky" and we had "Pie In the Sky Number Two" when we were down in the islands, and we built a beautiful theater on that last island we were on and the guys that projected the movies every night, here it is.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Can't see it on the microphone, but it is a great theater.

sp.speaker: William Liddy
sp.p: Now you see how that's closed.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Uh huh.

sp.speaker: William Liddy
sp.p: They started the movie, just pulled this down and there was this still a cover there.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Right?

sp.speaker: William Liddy
sp.p: And the screen, it come out on a track similar to your overhead garage doors.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Wow.

sp.speaker: William Liddy
sp.p: And they would start the movie through that filming.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Um hum.

sp.speaker: William Liddy
sp.p: Screen on to the screen and then they would park the screen, you know real dramatic, and then roll the white screen right on to the front of the stage.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Um hum, a real production?

sp.speaker: William Liddy
sp.p: Yeah, real production.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: The 75th SeaBees Memorial Theater?

sp.speaker: William Liddy
sp.p: Yeah, there's some of our shows.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: A collection of photos and shows?

sp.speaker: William Liddy
sp.p: Yeah, you see how our cartoonist represented.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Uh huh.

sp.speaker: William Liddy
sp.p: He was good. This is what he did for a living after he came home.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Oh, really?

sp.speaker: William Liddy
sp.p: Yeah he taught cartooning all over the country. Even went out to one of the colleges in California and taught a course out there for a while.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: What was his name again?

sp.speaker: William Liddy
sp.p: Jack Norris.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Jack Norris?

sp.speaker: William Liddy
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: That's great.

sp.speaker: William Liddy
sp.p: And, of course, like I say, we got along real good with the Philippinos. There's --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Oh yeah, Bob Hope.

sp.speaker: William Liddy
sp.p: Yeah, Randy, Randolph Scott --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Randolph Scott, Bob Hope and Thomas --

sp.speaker: William Liddy
sp.p: Yeah, we had Bob Hope --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Francis Langford --

sp.speaker: William Liddy
sp.p: Bob Hope, Francis Langford, yep --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Had them all.

sp.speaker: William Liddy
sp.p: Yep. And there was times they came there, what we called secure, there were still bombing raids going on, shelling going on. There was more than one time we had to stop a show and then go on with the show. They had their share of combat duty as well as us.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Well, very good, any other vivid memories come to mind?

sp.speaker: William Liddy
sp.p: No. Uh, I'm trying to think, well this Denny down here, from the 77th come upon the bomber strip. They had taken so much shelling that they had secured the field, sent all the pilots and planes out and we were in for some commendations, some medals, and so on. So they had us assemble up there on that bomber strip. Now they've got it secured because of being shelled, and here we are gathering to get our presentations on the same field that they've got secured. We're standing out there with our bare faces hanging out, getting medals, pins, and so on and so forth. The next day, they peppered that field with shells. The 77th had to go out and fix them up because it didn't take long to fix up a hole. Now I worked also in transportation every once in a while they would press me into service when they need drivers. So when we got on to Bougainville, yeah. We were unloading stuff from ships because everything had to come in on pontoon barges. The water was too shallow for the ships to come in anywhere and we were bringing in this pierce planking that they made the airfields out of. Now, each bundle of those weighed well over 500 pounds. So they sent us down to haul that stuff up to the airfield and they told us don't put any more than six bundles on. So I backed in, they were loading me up, crane loading up. When I got my six bundles on, I started out and the officer in charge, to this day I don't know what outfit he was from, he stepped in front of my truck and he said, "Whoa, whoa, where you going?" I says, "I got my load." He says, "You haven't got a load on there." I says, "I got a load according to the orders they gave me out of the motor pool. Well, he says, "You're gonna put more than that on." I said, "Sorry sir, I am going to disobey your order." I says, "Get away from in front of the truck because I'm leaving." So, I went immediately right to the motor pool rather than taking my load in. I told them down there. By the time I went on and unloaded my truck and came back, that officer had been replaced. Because any more than that you had to load it on the back end, so you almost had power steering without the power, you know, because the back end load, but that was about as much as that truck can hold, two-and-a-half ton was the maximum and, well, you could go 500 over. It wouldn't hurt but that pierce planking, six bundles of that was a load and it was a stake body six by six deuce and a half, that's one incident.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Other than that did you get along with the officers?

sp.speaker: William Liddy
sp.p: Oh, yeah, for the most part yeah, we had some good officers. One of our officers was from right out here in Painesville. His name is Sunday, I can't remember his first name, but for some reason or another he developed some kind of a fever and was shipped home before the rest of us and he was a civil engineer. And when we were on Bougainville after we set up camp, right behind us was graves registration or the cemetery, and one side of us was the anti-aircraft battery which I mentioned before and the other sides of us was an ammunition dump, so one night we got rousted out about 11 o'clock, got the call to get our truck and get our pumper and get down to the dump because the Japanese had hit it and everything was on fire, burning, going off, and of course, when it wasn't in the gun it could go any direction it wanted to. So we went down and they said, "Well, right now we can't use the pump, so park it and get out of here." In the meantime there was our dozers were down there shoving sand because that whole island is nothing but sand, on the level part anyway, and that ammunition was still going off the next morning but they finally got that subdued. One night Washer Machine Charlie come over and dropped his bombs and we had strung a fuel line between grave registration and our camp. It was on top of the ground to go up to a tank farmer where we had four tank, 4,000, 1,000 barrel tanks and they hit that. Luckily the fuel hasn't started flowing yet. It was dry but they hit that pipeline so it was always, it was just clamps to put it to go rubber rings and clamps, 20-foot lengths of pipe. We just took it out, put another piece in, that was it. And that 10,000 barrel tank I had mentioned we had put up at Torokina Point in Bougainville, they wanted to water test it so we were assigned the task of filling it with water from a little river, a creek is what it was really, and 76 hours straight of pumping, three shifts a day and we got that tank full. Well, they were building the moat around it so that in case it got ruptured it would contain the fuel and one of the dozer operators was operating a TD 18, International TD18 when has got a humongous blade on it for the size tractor it is. Unwielding, to tell the truth and instead of being straight down on the sides it was curved toward the bottom from the top, which made it wider at the bottom than at the top. So this friend of mine, he was down there pushing this sand up around the tank and when he started to back up he twisted around and a corner of the blade went through that 10,000 barrel tank about three feet off the ground. Seventy-six hours of pumping to fill that tank, and it emptied in a half hour, but they did get their test done because the tanks were put together in plates, sections bolted with rubber gaskets in between and that's what they were trying to see when they had pulled up tight enough on all them, they found all the leaks. And all those tanks were filled from 18 inches down to the bottom, was never used, that was for sediment water and so on that collected in there. That could be drained off. There was more than one when we had to go up and fill tank on the tank farm we built a tank farm that this seven spots, four times, 28 tanks to take care of that 10,000 barrel tank at the air field they'd fill that from a tanker and then pump it up to the air to the tank farm and one of my tasks while they were building that farm was operating a baby digger. It was built right over here at Cleveland Trencher and you had a five-foot circle on it. We were only going about two-and-a-half feet deep to put the line down underneath it, keep it from the fuel evaporating through the pipe in that hot sun so we had to put it underground. So there was one night there I was pumping that 18 inches of water out of the bottom of the tank and I had gone up there with a small pump on a two-wheel cart and pulled by a driving, a GMC dump truck. I wanted a Jeep but they were all in use, so I had to take a dump truck. So I was sitting there waiting for that pump to get through when we got a torrential rain. Well it drowned out the pump. So I couldn't get that going again and I didn't know how long was gonna last so I thought well, I better go down, back down to camp and then come back out if I have to. Well on my way back, when I got to the intersection, the crossroad, I thought, "Gee, that water is traveling pretty fast between here and that crossroad." So I had a long-handle shovel in the truck and in that driving rain I went out there and put the shovel down. What had happened is that the water was so fast and so much volume, it had washed out the road. Had I gone on, I'd have buried that truck, 'cause we built eight by eight ditches in order to take care of the water. So I crawled back in the cab, shut off the engine, went back to sleep. And the next morning about eight o'clock, they, somebody's hollering at me. "Hey you still over there, you still alive?" "Yeah yeah yeah." "We're approximate gonna come out pretty soon here and give you a couple loads of dirt so you can get back to camp." But they had to bring out culvert we used barrels cut out both of head and the bottom of the barrel and weld them, end to end, and then put them two wide, and two high, and made them about 40, 50 feet long, welded that all together and then drop that in that eight buy eight ditch. Well that had washed out too. So there was nothing for eight feet down, so they had to come out with a culvert first, drop it in place and then put a couple loads of dirt on so I could get across it and get back to camp. Little scrapes like that.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: William Liddy
sp.p: It was a good outfit though, the SeaBees, they're still, they're over in Afghanistan, they're in Iraq, they were in Bosnia. I went over, I am with Kaiser. I went over to get an MRI and a young fellow came out, called my name, you can follow me, I went in and he's filling out some papers and he says, he saw my cap.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Um hum, "SeaBees can do."

sp.speaker: William Liddy
sp.p: Yeah, and so he says, "You were in the SeaBees?" I says, "Yeah." He says, "When?" I say: World War II." He says, "Well, I just came back from Bosnia. And," he says, "I am within the Army and he says, "We were in a mud hole," he says, "We didn't have anything to eat, a hot meal in several days, we were eating out of cans." And he says, "Along come four five, truck loads of guys, all Seabees." He says, "Two days later, we had roads, gravel paths, We had a mess hall, we had a latrine, we had a shower room," he says, "You guys saved my life."

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: That's great.

sp.speaker: William Liddy
sp.p: Yeah. There was one of the guys that's a reservist in the SeaBees. He came down and gave us a talk. He had been in Kosovo and he had been there nine weeks and came back. It was just a short stint but they needed his expertise, so they called him in, and he came down and told us all about it. We had some good guest speakers down at our SeaBee meetings. We had the guys that were down and got the gunnet from the Monitor that was sunk, one of the divers came and told us all about him and the officer that was in charge. The two of them came in and gave us a talk and they had a slide show and that was interesting. They didn't want to bring the Monitor up. The reason they brought that gunnet placement up was because it was the first one that was a twin barrel and it revolved, it wasn't a fixed position. It was the first one that was made that way, so they have got that in a museum. We get some pretty interesting speakers down there. We've been short on them the last year.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Yeah?

sp.speaker: William Liddy
sp.p: We had a woman from down here from Chesterland that was part of the French Underground.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: I talked to her, Madam Totaris?

sp.speaker: William Liddy
sp.p: Margaret, yeah, yeah. I see her at the store every once in a while. She came down and talked to us. I had her come down here and talk to the kids at Kirkland School when we were talking to them. They called me and asked me if I could come in because in social science they were discussing World War II and they wanted to hear some first-hand accounts of it. So I organized a bunch of guys and we went down there and one guy from the Marine Corps, I had Bill Shell from the Air Force, had Roy from the LST, and me, and we spoke to two different classes. We were there all day, and you get talking and those kids are dead silent.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Yeah?

sp.speaker: William Liddy
sp.p: They asked some pretty good questions too. The girls always asked the questions, social things, how did you get along with the people? And the guys always want to know, how many times did you get close to a bomb going off?

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Yeah, right.

sp.speaker: William Liddy
sp.p: Well, one day we were standing, this was on Bougainville. We were standing around waiting for the trucks to take us out to our work stations, and they always say you never hear the bomb that kills you. You never hear the shell that hits you. We were all standing around talking and all of a sudden we here ZIP...BOOM. One guy says, "you know, that saying is pretty true," he says, "I never heard that thing until it hit and the thing is I'm lucky I heard it." Yeah, and it hit right in our camp. Luckily, it just hit a walking trail and it wasn't a very big shell. It was more than a nuisance thing. And to cause injury to people rather than blow anything up to amount to much. They sent a lot of those over. Oh, one of those nights that I was pumping water into that 10,000 barrel tank, I didn't know it because I was always on the late shift, I started at ten at night and got off at six in the morning. I didn't know that there was a gunnet placement company right next to us, right across the road from where we were pumping. Just a little guns I can't remember what they were but they only shot three miles. But I did see these posts over here with lights on them. One of these days I'm going to have to find out what that's all about. In the meantime I paid attention to whether my pump was pumping water, and I'm sitting there more or less day dreaming and all of a sudden, BOOM! That whole place next to me shot their shells. They had their gun right in their tent with them. They just rolled up the side of the tent and fired and dropped the cover again. That scared the living daylights out of me then. I thought I'd been hit. Then I found out what that was across there with all those little lights. Yeah, it was like a fence post with little white lights on the bottom, half inch in diameter and when that light was on, they were gonna fire, but I didn't know that until after it happened. Yeah, many is a time when I'm trying to get that six inch gun from Bougainville. We stood up on top of that 10,000 barrel tank, watch our planes take off, go over and bomb, come back and land, get another bomb on, take off, go over, bomb. We could watch them through the whole flights during their bomb run, their approach, back to landing at the airport, reloading. Standing up on top of that 10,000 barrel tank. Now, that air field we built has since gone under water.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Yeah?

sp.speaker: William Liddy
sp.p: Yeah, it was, we always thought it was on a shelf anyway, it felt like it was on a shelf and we were right. These paintings in here are done by our officers. That's Coral Sea Battle. Japanese ships, they tried beaching their ships. They tried to save their ships by beaching them.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Right?

sp.speaker: William Liddy
sp.p: But all they did was make a sitting target. See here.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Um hum?

sp.speaker: William Liddy
sp.p: This is Torokina Point. Now we put than 10,000 barrel tank right about here and we had a jetty out here, a wharf with a submerged line and a tanker came in and filled up the tank tied up to that. When we went into Bougainville, we followed the Marines wherever they went. And this is an island right across from that Torokina Point I just showed you.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Yeah?

sp.speaker: William Liddy
sp.p: We landed there while the Marines were fighting the Japanese. We could see and hear them.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Um hum.

sp.speaker: William Liddy
sp.p: And the next day we started moving our equipment across. There are the 1,000 barrel tanks being put up.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: William Liddy
sp.p: There's the 10,000 barrel tank.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Uh huh.

sp.speaker: William Liddy
sp.p: And we, yeah, you can see how it's going up.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: William Liddy
sp.p: There's one that's been hit, shrapnel hit it, see here's the line going in from out that little dock. See that ship there?

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Yeah?

sp.speaker: William Liddy
sp.p: I brought, took this book into the shop one day where I was working and a couple of the guys said, "I was down in the South Pacific." I said, "You want to see my book?" He says, "Yeah." Pretty soon he comes flying up to me and he says, "That's my boat!"

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Oh, great!

sp.speaker: William Liddy
sp.p: He says, "I didn't know, yeah, he says, "I was on a tanker, that's my boat," so gets to be a small world after awhile.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Oh yeah.

sp.speaker: William Liddy
sp.p: There, we had an active volcano.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Wow.

sp.speaker: William Liddy
sp.p: On Bougainville. And we didn't pay any attention to the smoke coming out of that thing. Here's one of the roads we built. It was 60-foot wide and on Christmas 1943, all of a sudden there was a rumbling, shaking first thing in the morning. I was always the last one to get up anyway. I thought somebody was trying to wake me up by shaking my bunk. They usually put their foot on your bunk and shake it like that. I said, "Okay, okay, I'm getting up." No answer. My eyes looked around, nobody there. We had dug down into the island four feet, filled the sand bags with what we dug out, put it up there, put our tent on top of that, left an island in the middle for the post for the center of the tent and air raids, we just stayed in bed, didn't need to bother to get up because we were in a foxhole anyway. So I got up and got out of that bed, out of my bunk and run up the steps, steps dug into the sand. Looked around and these big trees were just swaying like grass in the wind. That was their first earthquake.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Ha ha.

sp.speaker: William Liddy
sp.p: And a few days later, like I said, we got called into the motor pool every once in a while to help out. I was dumping some fill into a little gulley to make a path over to the shower room and wash room and I had just got the box up and the load was starting to come up when the truck started to move, I hit the brakes and I thought why am I rolling? Then I looked out, oh, another earthquake. The trees were swaying again. That had been any place where there had been some good solid buildings, they'd have been flattened.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: William Liddy
sp.p: Now this sign here, the Marines are pretty inventive themselves, they made that sign.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: (Reading sign) "So when we reach the Island of Japan with our caps at a jaunty tilt, we'll enter the City of Tokyo on the road the SeaBees built."

sp.speaker: William Liddy
sp.p: This is a famous picture. That's one of our officers from my outfit. This was built right up and installed up at the 77th SeaBees where Danny is, was from, and here's some of the things the Marines gave tribute, they gave to us for the help.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Signs, yeah.

sp.speaker: William Liddy
sp.p: And Denny says they went to bed one night there was nothing out there, they got up the next morning that sign was there, they never heard them doing it. They also told them, he said, remember Keith, what's his name, the actor, he died just a short time ago.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Brian Keith?

sp.speaker: William Liddy
sp.p: Brian Keith, yeah. He and a couple other guys had come up to his camp in a Jeep and were sitting out on a road. The one guy come in and talked to somebody he knew in there and a Japanese shell came in and hit that Jeep. Brian Keith and the other guy who had been standing near it but not up against it were blown clear across the ditch into the camp, must have been 40, 50 feet they were blown from the concussion. Then he says, "I got up and walked away, called in for transportation." He says, "They couldn't get any so we drove them back to the camp."

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Oh wow.

sp.speaker: William Liddy
sp.p: He was in the Marines. Yeah I saw a couple actors while I was there. Lou Ers, saw him in the Philippines. He was a conscientious objector. And so he did volunteer work wherever he could. Connected with the armed forces and he was working with a children's home when I saw him. And then there was Randy Scott. Joe Dereda. They had to stop the show because of the shelling one night and we set them up a stage on top of some barrels and built steps up to it, and that was it, that was their stage, that's how crude those things were. Yeah the, when we were up, we had what they called R and R. We went back at Mbanika in the Russell Islands. Rest and relaxation, yup, there was a gulley in the camp that we'd taken over. Someone has been there before you and the decks were still there so we built a theater. Coconut logs and a USO show came in, and a woman come out on stage dressed in a beautiful burgundy gown, strap -- spaghetti straps. She walked up to the microphone, sang her first song and she says after she got through, she says, "You got any other requests?" And the one guy from behind me hollered, "Yeah just stand there, Baby!" (Laughs). Yeah, we had guys that watched Bob Hope Show from in trees, they couldn't get anywhere near. Well, I stood on tip toes watching Oklahoma for two and a half hours. Oh boy, was I sore the next day. OH!

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Um hum.

sp.speaker: William Liddy
sp.p: We had some good shows. We saw Bob Hope twice.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: William Liddy
sp.p: The second time I wouldn't go to the show, the heck with it, I'm not going to stand on my tip toes any more.Thomas Swope:: Figured the jokes would be the same?

sp.speaker: William Liddy
sp.p: Because the guys started gathering in the afternoon for the evening show and about this time we got there what was after our work day and after evening chow, there was nowhere near, you couldn't get anywhere near the stage, it was loaded. The guys that had worked the night shift and were going to work the evening shift were the first ones there. Guys working the day shift, they don't stand a chance.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: William Liddy
sp.p: Yeah, when we went in any place we worked eight on, eight off, sometimes at first, it was four on, four off. You worked four hours, you had four hours rest, right back on again round the clock. You'd be unloading days, night, didn't matter, air raid come along. You'd quick shut off the lights, until Washer Machine Charlie decided to leave, and you went back to work again. And we knew it was, the area was secured when we had eight-hour shifts, six days a week.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Yeah?

sp.speaker: William Liddy
sp.p: And Sunday off (laughs).
